CHAPTER 5 
DETERMINING 
THE PARTIES' OBLIGATIONS UNDER THE CONTRACT 
significantly limit the use of the parol evidence rule to preclude enforcement 
f oral statements made to consumers that are negated by standard contract 
~erms. It states 
that 
"A standard 
contract 
term that 
contradicts, 
unreasonably limits, or fails to give the reasonably expected effect to a prior 
affirmation of fact or promise by the business does not constitute a final 
expression of the agreement regarding the subject matter of that term and 
does not have the effect under the parol evidence rule of discharging 
obligations that would otherwise arise as a result of the prior affirmation of 
fact or promise." Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 8 (Tent. Draft No. 2, 
2022), The potential benefit of this rule for consumers is obvious. What effect 
will it have, however, on businesses that use standard form contracts to 
assure that all of their transactions are governed by the same rules and may 
now face the prospect of litigation concerning what may or may not have 
been said by an employee or agent of the business? 
Bollinger v. Central Pennsylvania 
Quarry 
Stripping 
and Construction 
Co. 
Supreme Court of Pennsylvania, 
1967. 
425 Pa. 430, 229 A.2d 741. 
MUSMANNO, JUSTICE. Mahlon Bollinger and his wife, Vinetta 
C. 
Bollinger, filed an action in equity against the Central Pennsylvania 
Quarry Stripping Construction Company asking that a contract entered 
into between them be reformed so as to include therein a paragraph 
alleged to have been omitted by mutual mistake and that the agreement, 
as reformed, be enforced. 
The agreement, as executed, provided that the defendant was to be 
permitted to deposit on the property of the plaintiffs, construction waste 
as it engaged in work on the Pennsylvania Turnpike in the immediate 
vicinity of the plaintiffs' property. The Bollingers claimed that there had 
been a mutual understanding 
between them and the defendant 
that, 
prior to depositing such waste on the plaintiffs' property, the defendant 
would removE. the topsoil of the plaintiffs' property, pile on it the waste 
material and then restore the topsoil in a way to cover the deposited 
waste. The Bollingers 
averred that 
they had signed the 
written 
~greement without reading it because they assumed that the condition 
Just stated had been incorporated into the writing. 
When the defendant 
first began working in the vicinity of the 
plaintiffs' property, it did first remove the topsoil, deposited the waste on 
t?e bare land, and then replaced the topsoil. After a certain period of 
time, the defendant ceased doing this and the plaintiffs remonstrated. 
The defendant answered there was nothing in the written contract which 
required it to make a sandwich of its refuse between the bare earth and 
the topsoil. It was at this point that the plaintiffs discovered that that 
feature of the oral understanding 
had been omitted from the written 
contract. The plaintiff husband renewed his protest and the defendant's
